description: For a MARRIED borrower on an income-driven federal student loan plan, prices the filing-status decision: filing separately removes the spouse's income from the payment calculation, which lowers the monthly payment and often the lifetime cost by tens of thousands of dollars. Returns both sides with the monthly and lifetime difference. IMPORTANT: this models the LOAN side only. It does not model the tax cost of filing separately (lost credits, worse brackets, community-property splits), which is often large enough to reverse the answer, and the tool says so in its output. A balance and both incomes are enough: omit ratePct when the rate is not known and the federal rate for the loan type is used and stated. Use it whenever a married borrower asks about IDR, RAP, PSLF or how to file.

balance.description: Current federal loan balance in dollars.

borrowerAgi.description: The borrower's own annual adjusted gross income in dollars.

dependents.description: Number of qualifying dependents. A spouse is NOT a dependent.

loanType.description: Federal loan type. Drives plan eligibility, not just the rate.

loansMadeOnOrAfterJuly2026.description: Optional, default false. Set true when the borrower says the loans are new: first disbursed (or consolidated) on or after July 1, 2026. New loans can elect only RAP and the tiered Standard plan (Parent PLUS: the tiered Standard plan only), so leaving this false for new loans offers plans they cannot elect.

ratePct.description: Optional. Weighted average interest rate as a percentage, e.g. 6.54 for 6.54%. Omit it when the rate is not known (a linked account often shows the balance only): the 2026-27 federal rate for loanType is then used and stated in the answer (undergraduate Direct 6.52%, PLUS 9.07%; for graduate or professional Direct Unsubsidized loans pass 8.07). Required for a consolidation loan, which has no federal rate.

spouseAgi.description: The spouse's annual AGI in dollars. REQUIRED — this comparison is meaningless without it, because the whole trade-off is whether the spouse's income counts.

title: Compare filing jointly vs separately for student loans
